overview: This 1878 to 1914 map entry concerns coastal trading settlements and the expansion of French rule in what became Côte d’Ivoire. The colony was formally created on 10 March 1893, after the map’s opening date. Its people belonged to different communities with their own histories; a colonial name and outline cannot turn them into one timeless culture.

periods.title: Before the formal colony
periods.summary: The first map years precede the administrative creation of the French colony.

periods.title: Colonial expansion and changing towns
periods.summary: The formal colony dates from 1893. These dates describe this map record, not the full duration of colonial rule.

items.text: Grand-Bassam became the first colonial capital and an important port and trading centre. Its built landscape included a N’zima fishing village alongside districts assigned to administration, commerce and different populations. The town was both a place of everyday work and a physical expression of unequal colonial power.

Galleries, verandas and gardens helped adapt buildings to the tropical setting. African, European and Middle Eastern residents brought different experiences to the town. UNESCO describes both coexistence and conflict: the surviving streets should not be mistaken for a postcard of everyone living on equal terms.

sections.title: An elephant helps with the weaving

items.text: Baule and neighbouring Guro weavers were known for indigo-and-white cotton cloth. On a narrow-band loom, heddle pulleys helped lift and separate threads so a shuttle could pass between them. This small moving part made repeated work easier, while the weaver supplied the skill and rhythm.

One surviving Baule pulley has an elephant’s head. The museum dates it broadly from the nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century, so it cannot be assigned to a single map year. Carvers decorated tools used in public view: even a working loom could have a little elephant looking down.

A Baule comb from central Côte d’Ivoire carries a rooster above its teeth. Made from ivory and metal and dated to the nineteenth or twentieth century, it shows the care given to personal objects. Its owner is unknown; we should not invent a hairstyle, wedding or family story for it.

Gold-working traditions long preceded French rule. An older Akan brass weight, dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century and attributed to Ghana or Côte d’Ivoire, belongs to a regional system for weighing gold. Such objects were cast by replacing a wax model with molten metal inside a mould.

The decree creating the colony did not itself establish peaceful control over every settlement. Historian Christophe Wondji’s study of Bingerville describes opposition from local Ebrié residents and an uprising in 1903. Building a new administrative centre meant taking decisions over places where people already lived.

A 1911 medical report described repeated yellow-fever outbreaks on the Ivory Coast between 1899 and 1905. It reported that steamers avoided the port for four months in 1903. Illness affected travel, commerce and livelihoods as well as the patients themselves; a harbour could be busy one season and isolated the next.

The report described a change toward drainage and mosquito-control measures, replacing earlier practices that included burning houses. This is evidence of changing public-health ideas at the time. It is not a complete account of every household’s sanitation, and it cannot tell us which toilets an ordinary family used.

sections.title: Two dates on a piece of mail

items.text: A postcard caption describes loading mahogany onto the steamer Colonia at Grand-Bassam in September 1905. A message on its reverse is dated August 1906. These different dates distinguish the event represented from the later use of the card, an easy detail to miss when reading an old picture.

Another card carries “Embarquement des billes d’acajou”, meaning “Shipment of mahogany timber”. Its postmark reads 23 September 1907. This short French sample survives through the Smithsonian’s catalogue transcription. It records colonial printed language, not a greeting in one of the region’s African languages.

Wondji’s research shows that colonial planners argued over the relationship between an administrative capital and a commercial port. Merchants and officials wanted towns to serve the collection and export of products. That helps explain the competition among Grand-Bassam, Bingerville and Abidjan, beyond simply comparing their buildings.

ending.text: The 1914 map endpoint did not end French colonial rule. Côte d’Ivoire became independent on 7 August 1960. Grand-Bassam’s communities and crafts also continued beyond the colonial capital’s decline; political administration and the lives of a town do not share one ending date.
